question.problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{-3}$ can be used to transform the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={y}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{-3}\,⟹\,y={z}^{-1/3}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-3{y}^{-4}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{3{z}^{4/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3{z}^{4/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{4/3}}\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\frac{1}{{z}^{1/3}}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

We now write the above equation in standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x).
$$

In doing so, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x+3z\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-3z\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$
